utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before I give an opportunity to the Prosecution to call its next witness, I'd like to deliver a decision. But before doing so, I'll wait until the text is distributed to the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that's happening, may I reintroduce Mr. Andrej Jonovic. I'm delighted to say he's returned to the fold. The prodigal son returns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He's been on the team all this time; it's just that he's been away to a place called London. But we're delighted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, some people say London is the place for me, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It has been said, Your Honour. I feel it sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome. Then I'd like to deliver a decision. It is a decision on Witness Berko Zecevic. It's a decision on Witness Berko Zecevic pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Witness Zecevic is part of the fifth batch of 92 bis witnesses. The Chamber's decision with regard to this fifth batch will be issued early next week, but a decision regarding Mr. Zecevic has had to be prioritised since the Prosecution indicated that the witness would be available for cross-examination early next week if, of course, the Chamber would decide to call him for cross-examination. In accordance with both the Defence and the Prosecution submissions, the Chamber has decided to admit the requested material into evidence on the condition that the witness appears for cross-examination. The Defence's proposed redactions to the witness statement are not necessary, since the witness will be available for cross-examination. However, the last two paragraphs of the witness statement will not be admitted into evidence and must be redacted. The Prosecution agreed to the suggestion made by the Defence not to admit these last two paragraphs. This concludes the Chamber's decision on Witness Berko Zecevic. Then, Mr. Margetts, are you ready to call your next witness, who appears as a 92 bis witness, for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And there are no protective measures for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And it's the witness Bilal Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Which is reference 82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it, then, that you'll put just the questions necessary to introduce the material. Yes, of course there's no pseudonym sheet, but I take it that you want to confront him with the statement, then, first and then give him to the Defence for cross- examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Hasanovic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just one matter, and that is there are some contextual documents. I don't know whether the Court would like to receive those prior to the witness's evidence or subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends a bit on what it is and how important it is for the Chamber to have a look at it before we hear the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The documents are documents prepared by the Serb authorities in the municipality, and they may spark some area of inquiry from Your Honours. That's the only reason I raised it at this stage. From the Prosecution's perspective, we're content either --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- to introduce it earlier or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I take it that you've seen the list of contextual documents from which I do understand that two out of ten are already in evidence. That's P529, tab 322, and P455. Will there be -- could we expect any objections to this material?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then they could be distributed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. -- at least, I take it, Mr. Hasanovic. Before you give evidence in this court, you're required to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, you have been called mainly to be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: some statements you've given, but first some questions will be put to you by Mr. Margetts, counsel for the Prosecution, in relation to those statements. Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can just attend to the distribution of the documents, as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Numbers will be assigned at a later stage. You may proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness could be presented with a copy of his ICTY statements of 27 June 1997 and 8 November 2001. These documents have been tendered to the Registrar as part of the 92 bis package in CD format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be, Madam Registrar ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number for the statement dated 8th of November, 2001, will be Prosecution Exhibit P742. The witness statement dated 13 and 27 June 1997 will be Prosecution Exhibit P742A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If Mr. Hasanovic could be shown the 1997 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, since you've arrived in The Hague, have you had the opportunity to review this 1997 statement you provided to the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could I refer you to page 3 of the statement, where you refer to the persons who were appointed to regional courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you state that eight out of the ten regional courts were chaired by Serbs. Do you wish to correct that statement, and should that reference, in fact, be to the fact that eight out of the ten regional courts had presidents or public prosecutors who were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle this statement is correct. I wasn't going into whether there was one additional person there or one person less, but more -- this is more or less correct, since this information was published in the press at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can I refer you to page 6 of your statement, and in particular to the paragraph that starts: "On the 6th of May, Rajko Koprivica," and continues. And at line 5 of that statement -- of that paragraph, you state that you were asked to go to Sarajevo. Do you wish to correct that reference? And if so, what should that read?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Instead of "they asked me," it should read "they insisted that I go," or one should perhaps even say that "they ordered me to go."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasanovic. Apart from those two corrections, is the content of that 1997 statement true and correct in every particular?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I thought it had been amended by the subsequent statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart is perfectly correct, and in fact my question -- I'll withdraw the question, if I could, and refer the witness to the statement of 8 November 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, could you refer to the statement of 8 November 2001, wherein various corrections to your 1997 statement are set out. If I could ask you the question again: The 1997 statement that you've just reviewed, and in addition this 2001 statement, do they together, and also the corrections that we've just referred to in court, do they together set out your statement in -- correctly?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, whilst you're referring to this statement from 2001, could I refer you to the lists -- list of mosques that appears in this 2001 statement. Apart from the mosques listed there, were there any other mosques that were destroyed in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The mosque in Svrake is not listed here, in the village of Svrake, which is part of Semizovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, the Defence will you cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, unfortunately I did omit to read out the 92 bis summary, and my apologies for that, but if I could be given the opportunity to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hasanovic, Mr. Margetts will just read a summary of your statement, the statement which has been read by this Chamber. But since the public might not understand what the cross- examination is about, if we -- they have got no idea on the content of your statement. That's the reason why we read it out. It's not your statement, the statement is the one that's on paper. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In 1990, Professor Hasanovic was elected president of the Vogosca municipality. In 1991, around 56 per cent of the population in Vogosca was Muslim. In March 1992, the SDS delegates left the Vogosca Municipal Assembly without any substantial reasons or explanation. The SDS then insisted that Vogosca municipality be divided along ethnic principles. Although the Muslims knew that this could not be achieved, the Muslims participated in negotiations relating to the division in order to gain more time and delay any attack on Vogosca. On 5 April 1992, the conflict in Sarajevo began. In the second half of April, the police in Vogosca were divided. On the 2nd of May, 1992, Semizovac and Svrake were surrounded and shelled. On 4 May 1992, there was an air attack against Semizovac and Svrake. The residents surrendered their weapons, and 472 people, including women and children, were captured. The elderly people and women and children were released after two or three days; however, 200 men were kept in the barracks at Semizovac. On the 6th of May, 1992, Serb representatives, including Rajko Koprivica, approached Professor Hasanovic and demanded that he cross the front lines and attempt to find nine Serbs who had been captured by Muslim forces. They said that they would exchange the captured Muslims in Semizovac for these nine Serbs. On two occasions, Professor Hasanovic attempted to find the captured Serbs without success. Jovan Tintor stated that if anything happened to these nine Serbs, then he would kill all the Muslims in Vogosca. On the 17th of May, 1992, Professor Hasanovic was informed that his life was in danger, and he fled the municipality. 217 Muslims have been reported missing from the Vogosca municipality; of those, 117 bodies have been exhumed. 52 others are known to have been killed, and 48 are still considered missing. Most of the Muslim people from Vogosca left the municipality. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. Then, Mr. Stewart, you may proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, after the November 1990 elections, the position was this, wasn't it, that the SDA won 18 seats in the Municipality Assembly, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The SDS, 15.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the others took 18 seats.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that -- those others, one might broadly call them opposition, those 18, they operated as a bloc under the leadership of a Mr. Lazovic. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the composition of that bloc of 18 members, in terms of party, nationality?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I can now remember, nine or ten opposition deputies were of Serbian nationality; whereas, all the others were Muslims, Yugoslavs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you -- you say in your statement - this is paragraph 7 - that -- you refer to Mr. Koprivica as the SDS leader for Vogosca and the president of the Executive Board. Mr. Koprivica died last year, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, whether it was last year or within the last couple of years, do you know whether Mr. Koprivica has died?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. This is the first time I've heard about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you say anyway that you and he had a great deal to do with one another, he being the president of the Executive Board. The issues at the time from after the election in November 1990 through 1991, included in particular the conflict in Croatia. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The conflict in Croatia was one of the issues, among other things, but that was not the main subject of discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the main subject of discussion, then, between you and Mr. Koprivica?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The main subject of our discussions concerned issues dealt with by the Vogosca Municipal Assembly. Since we were the individuals with the greatest responsibilities in the Municipal Assembly, and there were really quite a lot of problems, quite a lot of issues, these are the subjects that we would most frequently discuss. Naturally, sometimes there were certain political issues that were discussed, but they were not discussed as frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you say that following the elections, the policy -- there was a division of functions within the municipal government. You -- you've said -- this is paragraph 9 of your statement -- that it was only the leading governmental functions which were divided according to party agreement and inside other municipality mercantile, commercial, and financial institutions in Vogosca, the Serbs were in the majority, and you've included in that by a correction administrative institutions. For example, Mr. Hasanovic, is it correct that of the five school directors in Vogosca, four were Muslims and one was -- classified himself or herself as a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that exactly now. If that is what I've said, then that is correct, that as far as the division of leading functions is concerned in the municipality itself, this was carried out on the basis of an agreement between the SDA and the SDS. As far as other officials and other posts in the Municipal Assembly are concerned, well, these positions were not divided; the staff remained the same. And as far as I can remember, two-thirds of the officials were of Serbian nationality and one- third, roughly speaking, were Muslims -- or rather, Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before we continue, you're referring to, I take it at least, to a numbered copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least the paragraphs are numbered. The Chamber has been provided with numbered copies for quite some time, but it seems that policy has changed again. It was very helpful to have numbers. Mr. Margetts, is there any reason why we got an unnumbered copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the thinking was that with the 89(F) statements, the numbered statements were provided, but with the 92 bis statements that has not always been the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say the originals were tendered. That's understandable. Mr. Stewart, could you please refer to pages and paragraphs on those pages so that the Chamber is better able to follow the cross- examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, of course I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I must say I'm slightly amazed that there should have been this change of policy. It was such an obvious practical help to everybody. I hope we shall revert immediately to the practice of having paragraph-numbered statements at all times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Will we be doing that, Your Honour? It's helpful to the Defence, as well as the Trial Chamber. Your Honour, I'm -- I'm asking whether that will be the practice, because it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, I've drawn the attention to it that it's helpful, and I take it that whoever is responsible for it will take care that we'll proceed in the most practical way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we're not going to interrupt at this moment. I've asked the attention for it, and let's now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, I didn't want to be misleading or tricking you a moment ago. You were under the impression, I think that, the point I put to you about the five school directors actually came from your statement. I want to make it clear it didn't. I'm not saying that you have said that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. You -- you've said you didn't remember. Can we take it you wouldn't dispute the proposition that five -- of the five school directors, four were Muslims and one Yugoslav? You don't say it's not true?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I won't say that it's not true, but all I can say is that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You -- you say in your statement - and this is the first paragraph at the top of page 3 - you say: "Even at that time" -- which appears to be immediately after the November 1990 elections -- "Serbs used to complain they were endangered by Bosniaks. They said they were threatened by Bosniaks. They used to repeat this very often in that period leading up to the aggression." Mr. Hasanovic, was it -- did their complaints include not so much physical aggression, but what they felt was unfair exploitation of the Muslim or Bosniak majority in Vogosca? Whether you agree with it or not, was that -- was that among their complaints?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it is true to say that such complaints were without foundation because the actual situation was quite different. I have already said in my statement that the Serbs mostly had the majority in the leading functions, in the economy, in the industry, not in all fields but in many fields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, I'd like to stop you. The question was whether the complaints did include the feeling of unfair exploitation and not just physical aggression. Your answer now explains why the complaints were right or wrong, but the question was about what these complaints included. And Mr. Stewart would like to hear from you whether it was physical aggression or physical aggression only, the question was not totally clear in that respect, but at least whether it also included an expression or feeling of being treated unfairly without physical aggression. Could you please answer that question, and may I ask you to concentrate very much on the precise question put to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I want to say is that no acts of physical aggression were committed by the Bosniaks -- or rather, the Muslims against the Serbs, but I believe that this was just a pretext that the Serbian side used to carry out the act of aggression that subsequently ensued. I don't know if I have been sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you have not answered the question. The question was not whether there was a good reason to complain about physical aggression. The question was whether these complaints were just about physical aggression, right or wrong - it might be the next question - or whether these complaints also included complaints about unfair treatment, exploitation, apart from any physical aggression. So we first are focussing on what these complaints actually were, and perhaps we'll then proceed with whether it had any grounds. But the first question is, Was it just complaints about physical aggression or did it also include unfair exploitation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that they complained that they were in a position in which they had to hand over some of their posts after the elections. They had to hand over some of their posts to the Bosniaks and to the Croats. It wasn't a matter of complaining about being threatened with acts of physical aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's an answer to the question. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it also correct that shortly after the November 1990 elections the Muslim community began to build a mosque in contravention of the zoning plan?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such information. I'm not aware of the fact that the Muslim side started building a mosque, apart from one building in the suburbs of Vogosca at that time or perhaps in 1991, they started building that building. I don't know whether this was done illegally or not; I believe that they had a relevant authorisation. But I do know that at the Assembly we reached an agreement. And since there was no Orthodox church in Vogosca at the time, we agreed to have an Orthodox church built in Vogosca and to have a mosque built in the town of Vogosca, since we didn't have a church and we didn't have a mosque in the town of Vogosca. This decision was taken at one Assembly session. Both decisions were taken at the same Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, whether actually, then, it was in contravention of the zoning plan, is it correct that there was a complaint by the Serb community that a mosque was being built by the Muslim -- obviously by the Muslim community in contravention of the zoning plan?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know that. I don't know what they've complained, but I really don't know what building it could have referred to except for this building that I've mentioned that was -- that the construction had started at that time. But it is a very small building in one of the suburbs, whereas all the other buildings were already in existence except for that one church and one mosque that I've referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there also a plan to build an Islamic centre in the village of Bradici?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: It's not an Islamic centre. It was just a small mosque, a regular small mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a complaint by the Serb community that that was being built illegally?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall at this moment whether they complained or not, but the fact that the construction work on that facility did start at that time probably might have been the reason. I mean, this building work started in this one part of the town of Vogosca and somebody must have noticed it, and they might have wondered, How come are they starting to build here now and there was nothing there before. And as to whether there were any documents there and whether there was anyone from the Executive Council presided over by Mr. Koprivica, they could perhaps tell you, because I had no insight into all the documentation at the Municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, is it correct that on the 1st of March, 1992, Muslims set up barricades at Kobilja Glava in the municipality of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of such barricades, but it is possible that something resembling barricades, some kind of checkpoints might have been there, but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you aware that at or very close to that time members of two groups - one called, known as the Green Berets and the other known as the Patriotic League - began to check documents, personal identification, and so on, of Serbs moving around the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that such groupings did indeed exist. But as far as I know, they checked everybody's documents, of all citizens moving around in the area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the particular area of Kobilja Glava, then, you say that members of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League were indiscriminately checking documents of Serbs and Muslims, do you?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know so or do you suppose so?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. I was not present in the course of such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you receive or hear of any complaints by Serbs that they were being harassed or discriminated against in this respect by members of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say - and this is the third complete paragraph on page 3 of your statement - as a -- it appears to be a fairly general proposition, the proposition after the elections, the last two sentences. You say: "We were very careful not to create a sort of frustration," -- that was in balancing posts -- "so we tried to resolve everything with discussions and agreements. I believe we really succeeded in that." Mr. Hasanovic, your perception there that you had succeeded in resolving everything with discussions and agreements, was that perception shared by the Serb community?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, at least on the basis of their statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did there come a point, then, at which that perception -- that was not the perception of the Serb community and it was clear that they did not regard everything as resolved by discussion and agreement?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: As to the distribution of roles, I don't think there were any problems there. Problems started cropping up later on after the SDS members left the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what date are we talking about there, then? March 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was March. I really can't give you a reliable date there, but I think it was March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 1st of March a young Muslim boy, a Kenan Demirovic was unhappily killed in Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Kenan Demirovic? Yes. Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that the Serb community held the view that he had been killed -- not deliberately murdered, but he had in fact been killed by Muslim fire? That -- that was their view, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that event to a certain extent, and I think that the comments coming from the Muslim side were exactly the opposite. That is to say, to the effect that this young man had been killed by Serbs at close range, since there were Serb houses very close to that place, and then they opened fire from those houses in the vicinity, and then he was killed. Probably it is extremely difficult to establish the absolute truth about the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hasanovic, I'm going to say straight away I'm not going to put for your agreement some definitive view on this, but the position is this, wasn't it, that there was -- there was at the very least some reasonable ground for the Serb suspicion that he had been killed by Muslim fire because he was walking through an area where Muslims with weapons were posted, and there was fire from weapons in the area that he was passing through? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: All these are assumptions. And as to the factual truth, well, I think at the time it was extremely difficult to establish that. So both sides stuck to their opinion, and probably it was the background to a certain amount of tension that started mounting between the Serb and the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hasanovic, I want to get to the nub on this one. The Muslims blamed the Serbs for the killing of this boy; the Serbs blamed the Muslims. Probably nobody will ever know. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it did enormously raise tensions, didn't it, between the two communities?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a certain amount of tension. I wouldn't say "enormous tension," but there was some considerable tension because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the young boy was buried two days later, on the 3rd of March, and shortly after that Muslims conducted an artillery attack on parts of Vogosca, Blagovac, Hotonj, Krivoglavci. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. This is the first time I've heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And very shortly after barricades were set up at the beginning of March by the Muslims. The Muslims demanded the dismissal of a number of Serbs from their offices, including Rajko Koprivica. That's correct, isn't it? Just a reminder, he was the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no official request, in that sense, from the representatives of the Muslim community at the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca. There might have been some individual voices calling for that, but I'm really not aware of that. And I mean, in the last analysis, why would Koprivica be held accountable for an accident like that, which could not have been checked and the facts could not have been established with 100 per cent certainty? But if I may add, the barricades you are referring to at Kobilja Glava were simply a response to the barricades set up by Serbs on the 1st of March around the municipality of Vogosca at both exits, in the direction of Sarajevo and Zenica. They set up those barricades there and they remained in place throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Isn't there on this as well, Mr. Hasanovic, an issue who put up barricades first and who was responding to whose barricades? Isn't that essentially the position?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that to a considerable extent this provides us with an answer to a number of questions or issues which arose later on, precisely after the setting up of those barricades on the 1st of March and the well- known referendum on the occasion of which the citizens of Vogosca voted in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was precisely at that time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, if you don't mind, I would like to stick to the sequence according to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before we -- we are close to a time for a break, but I'd like to ask you, Mr. Hasanovic: You're now giving your opinion on barricades: one in the direction of Sarajevo, at one end of the municipality, and the others on the other side of that municipality. You were asked earlier the following question: Mr. Hasanovic, is it correct that on the 1st of March, 1992, Muslims set up barricades at Kobilja Glava in the municipality of Vogosca? Your answer then was: "I don't know of such barricades, but it is possible that something resembling barricades, some kind of checkpoints, might have been there, but I am not aware of it." It's not easy to reconcile that answer with what you just told us, that there were barricades at the one end of the municipality in the direction of Sarajevo, Kobilja Glava, and at the other end. Would it not have been proper at the question to say, I'm aware that there were barricades but they were, as you know, told us, erected in response of barricades I -- erected somewhere else by the Serbs, rather than saying at the end, "I'm not aware of it"? Because it now turns out that, at least, you have some awareness of barricades, whether or not in response to other barricades. May I ask you, may I direct you to, in answer to questions, to tell us if asked about barricades what you know about them. We'll have a break until 11.00, and I'd like you to think this over during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart. Oh, the witness is not in yet. Could you, Madam Usher, escort Mr. Hasanovic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, just to round off from where His Honour's questions left the matter immediately before the break, whatever the reasons, can the Trial Chamber now take it that you do in fact know that Muslim barricades were set up in the vicinity of Kobilja Glava on the 1st of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is possible that there might have been a slight lack of precision in my answer because I'm making a distinction between the checkpoints and the barricades. In other words, the checkpoint -- well, a checkpoint is a place where you might have a place being manned by a number of people, armed or unarmed, checking out the passenger and transport movements. On the other hand, barricades are an obstacle to movement, something represented by lorries or some other technical or military equipment. Such a barricade existed as you went out from Vogosca to Hanicovac [phoen], and I had to go through there, through that barricade when it was set up. There were lorries and such like there. And as to the exit road from Vogosca, there wasn't a barricade of that sort, but it was a kind of checkpoint, such a checkpoint which I don't call a barricade, was also set up at Kobilja Glava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, let's stick with precision for the moment then. The answer that you gave, as quoted from the transcript by His Honour, had been: "I don't know of such barricades, but it was possible that something resembling barricades, some kind of checkpoints, might have been there, but I'm not aware of it." So it was quite clear you were telling the Trial Chamber that you were not aware of either barricades or checkpoints. But just to clarify now with precision, you are now saying something different, you'd accept, that you were aware of some sort of checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd like to return to the matter I was asking you about, then, about the question of dismissal of -- well, particularly Rajko Koprivica. You said that you were not aware of any official request. You did suggest there might have been some, let me call it, unofficial request. So again, I'm going to just press you for a little precision here, Mr. Hasanovic. Are you aware -- were you aware in March 1992 of any form of request by the Serb community in Vogosca - I beg your pardon - any form of request by the Muslim community for the dismissal of Mr. Koprivica as president of the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any request of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To perhaps jog your memory, do you recall a suggestion that Mr. Koprivica should be removed and replaced by the same Mr. Miro Lazovic [phoen] that was mentioned earlier in the course of this hearing this morning?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Such a request simply could not be taken into consideration since Mr. Koprivica and Miro Lazovic were from different political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, wasn't that --

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: And affiliations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] -- Mr. Hasanovic? Wasn't that precisely the point, that the Muslim community were suggesting that Mr. Koprivica, an SDS member, should be removed and replaced by Mr. Lazovic, who was in the opposition group?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just stress once again; I can't remember. It might have been the case, but I don't know at what level, from what side, but I believe that such a request would have been illogical and unjustified, at least at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, did you ever hear about such a request, formal, informal, whatever level? Did you ever hear someone saying that such a step should be taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't remember that now. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you are giving a lot of -- you say I've never heard about a formal request, then you say it might have been there, then you say, I do not know what level. That's all quite logical for someone who is at least aware that something of that kind has happened. Otherwise, you just might say I've never heard about it. But you're giving a lot of explanation, which suggests, at least, that the thought that such a thing would have happened is not entirely strange to you. So I'd like you just to ask -- I mean, there's nothing wrong or right on it, but I'd just like Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to know whether you ever heard, whether you have any knowledge, direct or indirect, of anyone insisting on such a step to be taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must reiterate once again, I don't remember that. But having said that, I can't rule out anything like that having happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course no one could rule out such a thing. You were asked about what you heard, what you saw, what you are aware of, and not to rule out anything you did not hear, you did not observe, you have not heard of. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Hasanovic, that the climate in Vogosca at the time, March 1992, was such that if any such suggestion was made, it would have provoked a -- a vigorous reaction from the Serb deputies in the Municipal Assembly, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what situation you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hasanovic, you were there. The situation I had in mind, just to clarify, was the position with whatever difficulties there were in Vogosca in March 1992. The -- the Serbs would have reacted strongly to such a suggestion, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Pardon? I thought I heard you say "yes" in your own language, Witness, but perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it was rather faint.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- can you confirm you had answered my question. I had heard you answer my question "da." Did Your Honour hear that as well? Because I --

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I heard. And I also hear now that the witness confirms it. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Hasanovic, so that there's no confusion, I am putting to you that it did happen and there was such a vigorous reaction. Does it follow from what you've said that you have no recollection of any such vigorous reaction by the Serb deputies?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your statement - and this is the first complete paragraph at page 4 - you say: "The first big conflict inside the Vogosca Municipal Assembly was in March of 1992. The delegates from the SDS party left the Assembly session without any reason or explanation." So just for the moment, just keep that in mind. The next paragraph, the first sentence, you say: "The SDS gave some reasons for leaving the Municipal Assembly." Now, I don't want to be unfair to you, Mr. Hasanovic. When we take together what you're saying there, you are saying that they did give some reasons, but you go on to say as far as you can remember, they weren't at all important reasons. That's what you've said. So can we start with your agreeing that they did in fact give some reasons?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And whether you regard them as important, whether you regarded them as important or not at the time, what reasons did they give?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, those are reasons of a political nature, considering that the SDS party members, who were also members of the Assembly, Municipal Assembly, had informed us that they got instructions from their leadership, I don't know whether the party leadership or some other body, I am not sure, that they had to leave the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca. That was the main reason. As to whether it was a justified reason or not, I wouldn't be able to say, but that was the essence of the matter. As far as I can remember, they did not dwell on it too much, but I believe it was the key reason put forward. They got instructions from above.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in your statement where you say the SDS gave some reasons for leaving the Municipal Assembly, but as far as you can remember they were not at all important reasons. So when you gave your statement you regarded the fact that the local deputies had received instructions from somewhere above as not important; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the Assembly of both Bosnia and Herzegovina and of Vogosca was based on the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that according to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, those reasons were not essential, considering the fact that those were requests put forward by one ethnic community whose attitude at that particular time was not based on the provisions of the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the SDS deputies in Vogosca give any local reasons for leaving the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any local requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when in your statement you referred to some reasons, and not all important reasons, the "some reasons" is -- is just that single basic reason of some sort of instructions from above; is it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what you refer to in that same paragraph, the second complete paragraph on page 4 of your statement, "a lot of discussions held on the level of Yugoslavia about constitution of new country," the -- now, Mr. Hasanovic, we've heard lots of evidence in this trial already that the simple position was, wasn't it, the simplified position, that the -- the Serbs didn't wish Bosnia and Herzegovina to leave Yugoslavia, did they?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was that -- whereas, the Muslim nation took a -- an opposite stance, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that difference was reflected or mirrored as a difference between the communities on the local Vogosca level as well, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say in the next paragraph - that's the third complete paragraph on page 4 of your statement - that "In March 1992 was when the SDS insisted we physically divide Vogosca municipality between the Bosniak side and the Serb side. In the end, the municipality wasn't divided, but they insisted on having discussions on the topic, forming one committee from the SDA party and one for the SDS." Mr. Hasanovic, the insistence on having discussions on the topic, that was a perfectly reasonable and sensible way to approach the issue, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Presumably the Serb side, on the basis of those claims, wanted to achieve certain political goals. First of all, the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina, starting with the division of municipal territories, which was something which we could not in principle agree to, but we accepted to hold talks. We wanted to find out what it was that the other side was insisting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, what I'm putting to you, Mr. Hasanovic, consistently with what you've just said is that the insistence of having discussions about it was entirely sensible and reasonable, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: A discussion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, in fact, you say Your Honours in the next paragraph, you say: "In a certain formal way, I supported that discussion." What -- when you say "in a certain formal way," Mr. Hasanovic, is -- is the position that you did support the idea of at least having a discussion?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you say: "In principle we accepted their energetic insistence on the division." We can take it, can we, that "we" is Muslim community and "their" energetic is Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in principle, you accepted their insistence on the division. Are you saying that your acceptance was, in fact, not your true view but was a position adopted by you ostensibly, the position you presented to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I feel I need to clarify this point. On a number of occasions representatives of the Serb side came to see me in my office, Slavko Jovanovic in particular, who was my predecessor as the president of the Municipal Assembly, and he tended to accuse me very often that I would be the one to blame if anything happened because we refused to talk about the division. It happened on a number of occasions. And within the SDA party we made the decision to accept the idea of talks to find out what the Serb side was after and to find out whether there was any common ground at all or not. That was our attitude, and on the basis of that attitude we went along with the idea of those talks, and we set up a committee which participated in this entire procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you refer to "three conditions" that you set down, the first, just seeking clarification: "We wanted to agree on arbitration, to arbitrating case of disputes in the division. We suggested the Supreme Court or a United Nations court." That was -- that condition had in mind arbitration by the Supreme Court or a United Nations court in relation to the division of Vogosca, did it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that concerned the division of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was a serious suggestion, was it, that a United Nations court might arbitrate on division of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your second condition - and that's in the next complete paragraph; it's the fifth complete paragraph on that page - was for "The SDS leadership to give us guarantees." And you're talking about the local SDS leadership in Vogosca there, aren't you, or are you? Which SDS leadership are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to both the local and republican SDS leadership. We requested to be informed of the official position of the BH SDS with regard to that matter, with regard to the issue as to whether the SDS within Bosnia and Herzegovina would agree to having municipalities divided in that manner, Vogosca and other municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and naturally we did not receive any such agreement from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that was a decision that you were imposing, but it obviously wasn't a condition that the local Serb leadership could deliver on their own, could they?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And your third condition, that "if the Cutilheiro Plan was signed we should bring our local agreements in line with that plan." Well, that would have happened automatically, wouldn't it, because the -- do you agree if the Cutilheiro Plan had been signed by all concerned, the Muslim leadership and the SDS, the Serb leadership, that local agreements would have had to have been brought into line with it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, these decisions would have been revoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the next complete paragraph, the one that begins: "We knew that actually such a division couldn't be made." In the second sentence you say: "We wanted to gain time so that the inhabitants could prepare themselves." When you say "we wanted to gain time so the inhabitants could prepare themselves," both the "we" and the "inhabitants," you're talking about the Muslim community, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and others, non-Serbs from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And "prepare themselves" includes preparation by way of arming, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Above all, that meant moving the local inhabitants to safer areas. That's what we had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which included arming, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Over the page in your statement - that's page 5 - it's the third complete paragraph. You say: "They wanted" -- the Serbs -- "They wanted to divide the police as well, even to accommodate the police in two different buildings. That process started to develop more quickly. The SDA really tried hard to avoid conflict as much as possible. It was a general SDS policy at that time to divide the police. The requests came from the top level down to the municipality." My question here, Mr. Hasanovic, is: What -- what do you personally, from your own direct knowledge, know, if anything, about such requests coming from the top level down to the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, apologies for interrupting. The transcript appears to be correct at page 32, line 12, but I didn't hear the reference to the "SDA" in that line. I heard a reference to the "SDS." I think Mr. Stewart may have misspoken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I could easily have done, but since my misspeaking - thank you, Mr. Margetts - since my misspeaking has apparently been picked up anyway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether it is clear in the translation for the witness, as well. So could you please, if there's any doubt, and there seems to be, that at least it's clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's even possible that Mr. Margetts misheard me, Your Honour, and I really correctly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can't do anything about it now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course. Of course we could start listening to the tapes, et cetera. But let's try to might clear. Yes. Yes. Yes. No, you're invited to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll repeat it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll read it again with great care.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- it's -- it says: "They wanted" -- that's the Serbs obviously. "They wanted to divide the police as well, even to accommodate the police in two different buildings. That process started to develop more quickly. The SDA really tried hard to avoid conflict as much as possible. It was a general SDS policy at that time to divide the police. The requests came from the top level down to the municipality." And my question was: What do you personally from your own direct knowledge know, if anything, about such requests coming from the top level down to the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I assume that these requests came from the top SDS level, so the local body in Vogosca, and they pursued the policies of their superiors, although we in the SDA tried to prevent such a division from being carried out because this would have been the beginning of a very difficult and chaotic situation, and even of a wartime situation. And that is what I could tell you about that very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hasanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hasanovic, would you please answer the question. The question was what you know personally about these orders coming from above. You started your answer saying: "Your Honours, I assume that these requests came from the top SDS level." So what Mr. Stewart is trying to find out is on what basis you assume that, whether you have any personal knowledge of such orders, and how they reached from the top to the lower levels. Could you please answer that question, because that was the gist of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, we received such information from the SDS, from representatives of the Serbian side in the Vogosca Municipal Assembly, and that is the information that I had access to and the information I can provide you with here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who told you? You say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This information was provided by SDS representatives who were in the Vogosca Municipal Assembly as well as their representatives in the police, since the police commander in Vogosca was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand. Could you tell us which representatives, SDS representatives, told you? All of them? One? Two? Five? And who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the names of those individuals now, but I know that whenever we discussed this problem, they always told us that they had received instructions from the top because these requests weren't made at the are local level. These requests were forwarded from the top, from the SDS, from the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also referred to SDS representatives in the police, since the police, as you said -- since the police commander, as you said, in Vogosca was a Serb. It's not clear here whether you heard that from the police commander or from any other police officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from the police commander. In fact, I should clarify something else. The chief of the Secretariat of the Interior in Vogosca municipality was a Bosniak; whereas, the police commander was a Serb. That was the result of an agreement after the elections. It was an agreement reached between the SDS and the SDA, and numerous discussions were held in the police station and in the municipality, other political representatives discussed these matters, and these matters were discussed at sessions of the Assembly in the municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, again, quite simple: You said the police commander. Who was that? And did he tell it to you, apart from where he -- just a simple question: Did he say so? And who was that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember his name now. That was a long time ago, 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember the name of the chief of the Secretariat of the Interior who you said was a Bosniak? Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember his name either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- you knew of Mr. Krajisnik, did you, at that time, in March 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you know what position he held in -- I'm not asking you now, but then in March 1992, did you know what position Mr. Krajisnik held?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was that position?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you ever -- you'd never met Mr. Krajisnik, had you?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you ever even seen him in person?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I had seen him on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know the -- do you know the nature of the charges against Mr. Krajisnik in this case?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether it's for me to now interpret the reasons for which charges have been levelled against Mr. Krajisnik. The Prosecutor is familiar with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's not the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, the question is whether you know what Mr. Krajisnik is accused of, or at least the nature of what he is accused of. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. If you know, please tell us. If you don't know, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to what happened in the course of the war in Vogosca itself, with regard to what the Serbian forces did, either the military forces or the volunteer forces, the persecution and the killing of individuals, the destruction of private buildings, religious buildings in the municipality of Vogosca, with regard to all these acts, well, I believe that this is what is at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hasanovic, I'll preface what I'm saying by saying at no point am I inviting you to express any opinion whatever on the validity of the charges against Mr. Krajisnik. In fact, with His Honour's permission, I'm distinctly asking you not to do that. There are only three people in this room and indeed in the world who have the responsibility of making those decisions, and those are Their Honours. The -- but you -- you know, do you, that Mr. Krajisnik is one person, at least, who is charged with being criminally responsible for a wide range of actions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, particularly in 1992, including killings, rapes, actions in detention camps, forced movements of population. You've mentioned, of course, yes, destruction of mosques. That -- that's -- that's enough to give the gist of the case against Mr. Krajisnik. You -- you know, do you, that that's what this case is about?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasanovic, when I say that Mr. Krajisnik is at least one person who is alleged to be responsible for those, I'm going to invite you -- no opinion to be expressed on the charges, Mr. Hasanovic, but I'm going to invite you to tell the Trial Chamber what you, just in a couple of sentences, what you understand to be the basis upon which Mr. Krajisnik is alleged to be responsible for all those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to such an opinion being sought from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, may I -- well, if necessary, Your Honour, may I indicate why I ask it? It may not be necessary, Your Honour. I -- if I can simply proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. You are not -- the objection is sustained. This is not a question that can be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in that case, Your Honour, I really must ask that I am allowed before an objection is sustained to give some explanation as to why I ask the question. That's only elementary fairness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why is not of importance, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is. It is of critical importance, Your Honour. It is of critical importance because it is a foundation and an entirely legitimate foundation for reasons that I'm -- if I'm given the opportunity of explaining to the Trial Chamber, I can explain to the Trial Chamber, and it is quite wrong that I should be deprived of such an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber cannot imagine any reason for such a question; therefore, at this moment the decision stands as it is. But if there would be a total lack of imagination on the side of the Chamber, you'll have an opportunity to explain that to the Chamber once the witness prior to the next break has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour. I don't allege a total lack of imagination, but I do, Your Honour, suggest a gap, which it would be appropriate for me to take some steps to -- to fill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, do you know that for a short time that Mr. Nikola Koljevic was involved in local politics in Vogosca, a short time in the middle of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: In the middle of 1992, no, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When do you say that hostilities first broke out in Vogosca? And I mean "hostilities" in an active physical sense, some form of fighting, military, paramilitary hostilities.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, with the exception of certain incidents, armed conflict in Vogosca broke out on the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know that on April the 18th, near the Pretis factory in Vogosca, there was a serious clash between Serb forces and Muslim paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of the fact. However, the forces were not paramilitary ones, these were regular forces from the BH Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who was their leader?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the TO at the time was Colonel Hasan Efendic. He was officially the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who was Jusuf Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I have very little information about Juka Prazina. I know that he had a unit of his own in Sarajevo. As to the kind of the unit concerned, as to whether he was a TO member or whether he was some kind of a maverick, I really don't know. But all I know is that he came to a tragic end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Wasn't he the leader of a Muslim paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Where exactly? Are you referring to the town of Sarajevo or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, wasn't he the leader of a paramilitary group of Muslims that was involved in this clash near the Pretis factory on April the 18th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You had heard of him obviously from your answer.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you hear of him in March and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do the following names mean anything to you, Mr. Hasanovic: Zeljko Dzeremaja and Dalija Vladusic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Branko and Ranko Sikiras?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know those surnames.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Milorad and Ranko Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I came across these surnames in some sort of written documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Milan Pajdak?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Jovo Zivkovic?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Those are nine names that I have given you, Mr. Hasanovic. Are they not the same nine Serbs referred to on page 6 of your statement in the very long paragraph on that page that begins: "On May the 6th, Rajko Koprivica, president of the Executive Council, Slavko Jovanovic, and one or two other persons came to my house, told me that the BiH Territorial Defence controlling the territory between Kobilja Glava and Hotonj had captured nine Serbs on May the 4th"? Those are those nine Serbs, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I can't remember all the names. I can only remember Sikiras. And as for the others, well, I can remember them when one reads out their names for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you now accept that those are, so far as you can remember, those nine Serbs that are talked about in several paragraphs, passages, in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have a list at home, a list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is one of them the brother of Jovan Tintor's wife?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On page 7 of your statement, second paragraph, you say: "There were a" -- I think you slightly corrected -- "There were several improvised prisons in the city" -- we're talking about Sarajevo -- "And I couldn't find any names on any of those lists. I did see the name of the brother of" -- it says "Jovo Tintor" but it's the same Tintor -- "Jovo Tintor's wife, though." So you saw the name, but you're now saying you don't know the name?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall making a statement to the effect that I had come across the name of Jovan Tintor's brother-in-law anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You better be given the B/C/S version of your statement, then, please, Mr. Hasanovic. You may already have it in hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't know whether anybody on the Prosecution side can help us to steer the witness very quickly to the equivalent paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We'll make our best efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You should be able to find somewhere on about the fifth/sixth page of the statement a very long paragraph that starts: "On May the 6th, Rajko Koprivica." Do you -- can you find that to start with? It's about 20 lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about page 6, the big paragraph in the middle?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's the one I'm -- that's precisely the one I'm talking about, Your Honour. But please remember the witness has the B/C/S version, where the page numbering may be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry, Your Honour. You have the advantage. I just didn't know what page it was on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's page 6, Mr. Hasanovic. And the particular paragraph -- the particular paragraph is at the top of page 7. We found it now, Your Honour, from Mr. Krajisnik. So the first paragraph on page 7 of the B/C/S is the one that -- precisely the one that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you see -- I'm now reading from the English, of course, Mr. Hasanovic, which you're getting in translation, but it should match: "There were several improvised prisons in the city, and I couldn't find any names on any of those lists. I did see the name of the brother of" -- it says "Jovo Tintor," but that's -- can we confirm that's the same person? That's -- that's Jovan Tintor, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- so at that time you knew the name because you saw it. So in that list of nine names that I've given you, are you saying now that you don't recognise any of those nine names as being the name of the brother of Jovan Tintor?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That name was indeed on the list of nine names that I was given by the representatives of the Serb side at Vogosca. And at the time, I knew that man's name, his first name and his surname, but I can't remember now. I do remember that there was a list and that there was a family name, Sikiras there. So it was a list that was given to me at a later stage by the Serb side because the representatives of the Territorial Defence Staff from Kobilja Glava and Vogosca, they were unable to give me the names. I got the names the next day from the Serb representatives at Vogosca. And I did not say that I found this gentleman that we are talking about somewhere on another list, a list of those arrested in the city itself, in Sarajevo, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you -- and you met Mr. Tintor personally over this issue, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a meeting with Tintor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he was angry and upset about his brother-in-law, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I remember that Tintor was on that committee for the talks that we had between the SDS and SDA at Vogosca, and I think those talks started after the 18th of April, 1992, but I can't remember exactly whether I had an actual meeting with him at that time. There were several of them from the Serb group at Vogosca that I was in touch with. As to whether Tintor was a part of that group or not, I can't confirm at this stage. But I do know later on when I left Vogosca I had a phone conversation with him in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, I asked you really a very simple question, that -- I said: "Mr. Tintor was angry and upset about his brother-in-law, wasn't he"? Can I -- may I have an answer simply to that question?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Because obviously through other representatives of the Serb side I did hear that he was angry about it, which is altogether normal and natural. And as to whether I actually did see him and had an actual conversation with him in person at that stage, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was Boro Pradic?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: What I know about that man was that he was in charge of some kind of independent group at Vogosca, some kind of voluntary group, and in a way he was spreading fear and terror within Vogosca itself. But as far as I can remember, he was also somehow neutral in terms of -- or independent in his actions. So in a way he instilled fear not only into Serbs but into Muslims, as well. And I can confirm that because of the fact that on one day - I can't remember what date it was - he shot at the police commander in Vogosca, who was a Serb. He wounded him, I think in his leg, left or right. And he was lying in the street for as long as half an hour in front of the police station at Vogosca, according to my information, and nobody dared approach him. Afterwards he was taken to hospital in Sarajevo at -- he was at Kosevo Hospital, and I visited him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He was -- he was the leader of a bunch of paramilitaries who were engaged in terrorising out-of-control activity under nobody in particular's direction, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: As to whether he was being under anyone's control or not, I don't know, but the wounding of the police commander seems to indicate that he was indeed independent, because otherwise what sense would it make to wound somebody who's on your side. But as to whether he was a part of any superimposed structure above himself, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When did you visit him in hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Visit who, actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand the testimony to be that the one that was shot at was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry. I beg your pardon. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When did you visit the -- the police -- the wounded police commander in hospital?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date. After the wounding. The next day or two days later. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
