utterances.text: And do you remember that Boro Pradic himself was killed?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it correct that the group that was under his leadership had already been dissolved before his death?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you -- do you recall that there were in Vogosca throughout the period of hostilities what are known as weekend fighters?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what I'm putting to you: These are people who -- who came from outside, would come in as the weekend implies, but would come in for two or three days perhaps, cause trouble, perpetrate aggression, and then go away again. Do you recall anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I heard of such groupings, but as to how they came, in what way, with whose approval, I don't know. Because someone would have had to give them the go-ahead, to first of all come and then leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you say in your own statement - this is the top of page 6 of the English, the second paragraph - "Things were very confused." Now, that's an understatement, Mr. Hasanovic, isn't it? Things were extremely confused, disruptive -- or disrupted, with all sorts of fighting going on, with all sorts of groups, Muslims and Serbs in Vogosca in April/May/June 1992. That was the position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to the situation up until the 2nd of May, 1992. Up until then, in the area of the municipality of Vogosca, there was no open armed conflict. The situation was extremely tense and very chaotic and difficult. People had stopped working in factories, and the industry was quite well-developed there, and many people used to work in the industry, but everything came to a halt, and people would just sit in the park and comment on what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know that at the same time that those nine Serbs were captured, on May the 4th, that Muslim forces or -- or around the same time Muslim forces had entered an unprotected village of Grahoviste and killed 20 civilian Serbs, mostly women?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that those nine citizens of Serb nationality were arrested at the village of Grahoviste. And as to the information that either -- before or after the armed forces, the Territorial Defence, or I don't know who else, entered that village and killed 20 people of Serb nationality, is something I had never heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you don't personally know about those nine men being killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've never seen any of them ever again, have you?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know any of them in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any of them still being alive since 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Vogosca had its telephone lines and electricity cut off for a substantial period of 1992, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: There were occasional power cuts, and that refers to both electricity and the cutting of telephone lines. But afterwards, ever more often actually, it tended to last longer, especially after March. Throughout that period, those power cuts tended to get longer and longer. And on the 2nd of May, the situation was very critical when it came to energy supplies, telephone lines and all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the main water reservoir in -- for Vogosca in Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It might be wrong if I say either yes or no. I know that for the most part probably Vogosca got its water supplies from the main source of the River Bosna, below Igman near Sarajevo. And to a certain extent the supplies came from some minor sources in the vicinity of Vogosca itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There was a reservoir at Kobilja Glava, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, there must be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, are you saying -- you were president of this municipality. Are you saying you don't know whether there was a reservoir in Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: It is more of a political role, the president of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Municipality, and the executive body is the actual Executive Committee headed by Mr. Koprivica, and they were in charge with all these technical - -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation]-- matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, do you know whether there was a reservoir in Kobilja Glava?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Kobilja Glava under Muslim control throughout the period of hostilities in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Even if you don't know where there was the reservoir, do you know anything about Muslims cutting off the water supply into any part of Vogosca in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So as a result of the various answers you've given, if I suggest to you that Muslims in control of Kobilja Glava cut off the water supply from the main reservoir, as a result of all the answers you've given you say, I don't know anything about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was Ejup Demirovic?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can remind me a little bit, jog my memory a bit, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. I'll jog your memory with this: He was the leader of the forces that attacked the village of Grahoviste on the 4th of May, 1992. Does that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was the commander, but I do know who was the commander of the Territorial Staff at Vogosca at the time. And who led this particular group, I don't know. And this name, Demirovic, means nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So this particular group that was led by somebody whose name you don't know, you do at least know about that group?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I know of a group of Serbs who were arrested. And who was the leader of that group, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could I just ask you how much time you'd still need for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think about ten minutes perhaps, Your Honour, something like that. It depends on the answers, as always, but something in that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to refer to a couple of documents in re-examination, and that may provoke further questions from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber very much would like to finish with this witness today. We will have a short break, but I'd first like to ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not entirely clear to the Chamber what the line of questioning -- in what way the line of questioning in cross- examination assists the Chamber. Are you establishing a different picture as to the background of the conflict in Vogosca, or are you actually asking the Chamber to consider that it was -- whatever, what happened in Vogosca was in self-defence or was justified? It's rather unclear to the Chamber. You've got one minute to briefly explain what the relevance of the line of questioning is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's more the first than the second, Your Honour. I can explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's the ten-second answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a legitimate background --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you very much for that answer. Then the next item is that you wanted to explain why you want to ask the witness what he understood to be the basis upon which Mr. Krajisnik was alleged to be responsible for all those matters. You have -- as I said, the Chamber always considers the possibility that it lacks sufficient imagination. You have one minute to explain that and we'll consider it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it's this: The witness gave an answer about orders or directions coming from the top in which he specifically mentioned the Assembly, a point which he'd certainly not mentioned in his statement. And, Your Honour, the purpose of my question is to explore the witness's awareness that the Assembly -- or to the extent to which the Assembly and Mr. Krajisnik's position in the Assembly underlies this case and these charges against Mr. Krajisnik, because that is absolutely capable of casting light on the reliability of the witness's incorporation into his answer of a specific reference to the Assembly as one of the places from which orders or directions from the top may have proceeded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that is directly relevant, Your Honour. The witness's understanding in relation to that matter is -- is a clear foundation of that entirely legitimate exploration of an answer he has specifically given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give me the line where the witness said that the instructions came from the top so that I can find --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It will take a moment to find it because the problem -- I had it there in front of me, Your Honour, when this came up. It's now gone and my team are finding it. It was -- it was at that time when -- immediately before that exchange. So it was about, I don't know, half an hour ago or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have two references where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- this matter was discussed. First page 27, lines 1 to 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see on page 35, lines 3 and 4, where it says: "These requests were forwarded from the top, from the SDS, from the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's the reference almost simply that I had in mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I just look at it on my screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 35, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "These requests were forwarded from the top, from the SDS, from the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's precisely -- that's the very point and the very passage that I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Thank you for that. Mr. Krajisnik, you've heard Mr. Stewart would need another ten minutes approximately. Would you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Stewart has already asked me, and I told him that when he is finished I'll be pleased if I have no further questions, but I am undecided to ask questions in case anything is forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course you -- I can imagine that you do not now know exactly whether, after 10 further minutes of cross- examination, the situation is still the same. Mr. Margetts, how much time would you need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to present three documents to the witness and -- and receive his comments. Probably 10 to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten to fifteen minutes. Because the Chamber very much would like to finish with this witness today. We'll have a break of 20 minutes. We'll start again at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Stewart, you'll have another 10 minutes, of course, depending on how it develops. And at the same time, the Chamber informs you that you have made your point, that even if the witness does not give many details, that violent clashes in the early stages were certainly not the exclusive domain of one party. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And on the other matter, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other matter, the ruling stays as it is. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. May I just pick up where I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also in the next 10 minutes there's no need to go into any further detail on the matter I just mentioned, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, on the answer at page 34, Your Honour, the - - the answer which was the basis of my point, or did Your Honour mean something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I was saying that there's no need to go much further in the background during the next 10 minutes. And as far as the other matter was concerned, the ruling that the objection was sustained has not changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that's what I understood, Your Honour. I wasn't proposing to go any further anyway in relation to the background issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But I was understanding that Your Honour is not now suggesting that I can't explore that answer at page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, when you were talking in your evidence about an hour ago, perhaps it was, about local SDS Serb leaders in your municipality receiving instructions from the top, you said: "These requests were forwarded from the top, from the SDS, from the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Now, are you saying that you remember that somebody told you specifically that instructions or requests to local Serb leaders in Vogosca had been received from the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I answer the question, if you will allow me, I would like to go back a little. I just remembered the persons that you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... may I ask why the witness should be granted permission to go back a little as opposed to simply answering the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, if you would first answer that question. But I did understand from what you said that something came into your mind that was dealt with earlier and that it's now clear in your mind. But please first answer the question, and then you'll come back to the other matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received this information from SDS representatives; I can't remember the individuals who told me that. In any case, we did receive reliable information from SDS representatives. They told us that they were instructed to walk out from the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, what I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not the question, Mr. Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you could repeat the question, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But may I ask you to focus very much on what the question is and to answer that question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I'll slightly rephrase it and try to get it absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, are you saying you remember that somebody told you that a request or instruction had been received in Vogosca from the Assembly of the Serb Republic?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't mention the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I may have mentioned that it was the top of the leadership. However, SDS members told me that they had been instructed to do that by their top leadership. But if we are talking about the Assembly, then I believe that the instructions had come to them from the Assembly of the Serbian People that had been established before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What is the basis, the factual basis, of your belief that the instructions had come from the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that SDS representatives told us those things in the Municipal Assembly of Vogosca. I don't have any other information; I don't have anything else to give you, no documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, I'm inviting you to make things clear. In an answer you gave just a moment ago, I asked you whether you were saying you remembered that somebody told you a request or instruction had been received in Vogosca from the Assembly. You answered that by saying, "No, I didn't mention the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I may have mentioned it was the top of the leadership," which, if I'm allowed to suggest an understanding, seemed to make it clear that it was top leadership generally and nothing specific about the Assembly. Now you're saying, apparently, that the SDS representatives told you something on which you based your belief that the instructions had come from the Assembly. Now, Mr. Hasanovic, are you saying that you've -- you're just make some assumption or inference that top leadership included the Assembly or that there is some specific factual basis for your belief that instructions came from the Assembly? Which -- which of those is it? Is it an assumption or an inference, or do you know something specific that tells you that instructions came from the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any other information apart from the information that I've already shared with you, and this is what I base my opinion on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you: Did they tell you that it came from the leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they did tell us that it had arrived from their leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they give any further specification of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We discussed the whole thing, but the details of those discussions escape me at the moment. We were very much interested in this issue of them walking out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to know whether during such discussions or whether they gave any further details as that they received instructions from the -- as you call it, the SDS leadership. Did they, during these discussions, debate -- did they give any further details; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told us that they had been given instructions from the top. I don't recall any other details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That covers the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you make a difference between the instruction of the SDS and those in the leadership and the higher members of the SDS, those in the higher echelons of the SDS? What distinction do you make there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is a difference, that the SDS is a political party and the Assembly is a legislative body, but there's also coordination between these two bodies, given the fact that the Assembly was the Assembly of the Serbian People. So it would be normal to expect from the SDS, as a political body, to exert a certain influence on the way decisions are made in the Assembly itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, despite the injunction only very rarely to intervene on Judge's questions -- but, Your Honour, may I say I'm entitled to intervene when the answer is beyond the scope of what the witness should procedural be giving evidence about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to Judge Hanoteau to deal with the matter. I do understand that he would like to continue. Judge Hanoteau, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do have an objection to the answer as it's proceeding now on that basis. Of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This will be handled by Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like for you to clarify. You have just told us that the instructions came from the top; I would like you to clarify this top. The top, when you say "the top," is this the Assembly or is it the SDS party or is that one in the same thing for you, when you say "the top"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I include all of the above, all of the bodies that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean that you mix the two? When you say that the instructions came from the top, for you this is both the SDS and the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't claim for a fact that it was either the SDS or the Assembly, but I believe that there was coordination between the SDS and the Assembly when such decisions were in question. As to who exactly sent these instructions down the line to the lower-level bodies, I don't know. I can only assume. I believe that it was the Assembly if the instruction was sent to the lower-level Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a general rule in this courtroom, Mr. Stewart and Mr. Harmon, whenever there's any intervening in the question of the Judges, that will be dealt with by the Judge who is putting the question at that moment to the witness. That is just as a general procedural guideline. Here again, Mr. Stewart, there were a lot of beliefs and assumptions in the last and there were also elements that say "I do not know, but". Well, even at a certain moment, I noticed that "I can't claim for a fact." That's clear language. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- Your Honour, I understand the signal, but I was going to ask just one more question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, so far as other people in Vogosca told you that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they had received any communication from their top leadership, they didn't tell you whether their top leadership in their minds meant this particular organ or that particular organ or the Assembly or whatever organ of Republika Srpska, did they?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: It is quite possible that they told us at the time. However, as I sit here, I can't remember. It was 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanovic, this might be the opportunity. You were a few minutes ago going to say, I think, that you had recalled something about those -- those men. That was another topic. I stopped you then, but this might be the opportunity for you to come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, when I invited you to first answer the question of Mr. Stewart, you had something on your mind. Please share it with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was reminiscing on those times, some names came back to me. I don't know whether that is important at this moment. The police commander's name was Boro; I don't remember his family name. And the chief of the Secretariat for Defence was Elvedin, and I believe that his family name was Mehic. This is what I wanted to share with you, the names that I wanted to give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm nearly there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the TO, Territorial Defence, in Vogosca in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your statement, on the last page it is in the English version, there's a paragraph that begins: "217 civilians from the municipality of Vogosca." In fact, I think you've corrected the figure to 250. So it's now "250 civilians from the --

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- municipality of Vogosca have been reported missing as a result of the ethnic cleansing." Now, first of all, is it correct that the -- the reports or the report is a report of a number of civilians missing, rather than a report which includes the statement that it is a result of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: This information was published in a book, the book that was published in 2001. And it describes the events in the territory of Vogosca. The information had been collected by the Institute for the Investigation of War Crimes based in Sarajevo, and this is a state institution in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what -- when you say in this bit of your statement that 250 civilians had been reported missing as a result of the ethnic cleansing, what you're doing there is recording a report of which you are aware, as opposed to your own actual knowledge.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- you agree, do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just -- the three professional Judges on this Bench, if they are informed through a testimony about a report where a certain number of people are missing, whether it says "ethnic cleansing" or not, of course the Chamber will understand the "missing" to be in the context of the events that happened in Vogosca. And whether that is ethnic cleansing, yes or no, is of course not established on the basis of a qualification given in such a report. The Chamber will by itself consider whether that's the case, if at all relevant to establish that this was ethnic cleansing or whether you should use other terms or whatever. But I hope that you're confident that this Chamber will not, on the basis of a qualification given in a report it has not yet even seen, say, Well, ethnic cleansing because it says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, indeed. And then this witness's -- if you like, this witness's position is one further stage removed. So -- so on that basis, Your Honour, I am sufficiently confident not to explore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Your Honour just gives me one moment. I think I'm there, but if I may just double-check. Yes, I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Krajisnik, do you have any questions for the witness? Because, Mr. Hasanovic, we allow Mr. Krajisnik, who is the accused in this case, to ask additional questions to witnesses if there's any need to do so. Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although Mr. Stewart has examined the witness quite thoroughly, I will take the opportunity and put several questions to the witness, and I will try and leave some time for the Trial Chamber as well, as well as the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Hasanovic. We are speaking the same language, which you call Bosnian and I call Serbian, and could you please make a break between my question and your answer so as to allow for a better understanding in the courtroom. I'll start with a somewhat odd question: At one point you said - and you explained how you left Vogosca - and you said that you prayed to God. And as a church-going person, could you please tell us whether you now still believe that it was God who saved you and allowed you to leave Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm glad to hear that. Secondly, this makes me believe that you will answer my questions truthfully. You know the late Mr. Izetbegovic. Did you read this book of his?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Halilovic, who is an indictee here, and are you familiar with his crafty strategics?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't read the book. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Since you haven't read these books, I'm not going to ask you about the contents of these books, but I would like to ask you something about Mr. Izetbegovic, with all due respect to him. When you joined the Presidency to ask for the nine kidnapped Serbs, did you truly want to find them? Was that really your intention?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You asked the president of the Commission of the Presidency whether you would be able to find them. Are you convinced that they answered you truly to the best of their knowledge that they didn't know where these Serbs were?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were honest when they said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well, then. Just a small digression here. In our language, we use the word "speculation," which is not a positive thing. In English, that is asking for your opinion. So when I say "speculation", I'm not negative. I am asking for your opinion. I would like you to speculate and say that if you had had an opportunity to talk to Mr. Izetbegovic at the time and if you had asked him to help you ask these nine people, do you think that Mr. Izetbegovic would have done that?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I am deeply convinced that he would have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: This is why: When I spoke to the members of the commission and when I handed over the information to the Republican Commission for Exchanges of the arrested and killed persons, I did address the office of President Izetbegovic and his daughter, who was the head of his office. I knew her personally because we had taught school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: And I asked her to get involved in the issue and to talk to President Izetbegovic and other people and make sure that those people were found as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Again I'm calling for your speculation, that is, for your opinion. Why do you think he didn't do that, although we both believe that he would have done that if he could have? Why do you think he didn't find those people?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't really speculate or anything. I can't assume anything. I don't know whether he had any information about these people and to what extent he took an interest. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I do apologise. You said that you were sure that he would have done his best to find them. So you assume that he would have tried to find them.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I am familiar with the ethical principles on the part of Mr. Izetbegovic to the extent that I knew him, I believe that on his part he would have done everything he could in order to find these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: May I put to you a question that I would like you to answer with a yes or no: Are you telling me that Mr. Izetbegovic could not get at that information because there were lots of prisons there, there was a general state of chaos, there was a war going on, and he just could not get that information?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can only assume --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, speculate. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: -- that through his cabinet - and they did it through the competent state committee - insisted for those people to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: But we're talking about 2 square kilometres here in Sarajevo. It's a small area, maybe 3 or 4 perhaps. It really doesn't matter. Can you confirm it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a bit more. I disagree. We have Ilidza and the city hall and a bit -- it's much, much more than you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Tell me how much.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't speculate on that. It is not 100 square kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No. So could Mr. Izetbegovic know what was going on Kladusa, Tuzla, and some other places if we are saying that he could not know what was going on in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: What he could or could not know is something I can't tell you on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: All right, then. And now, can you speculate on something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you know where is Vogosca? May I just finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you may not finish. For the third or the fourth time you clearly indicated in your question that you're calling for speculation, and you asked questions on facts the witness is aware of, not on speculations. The fact is in relation to the matter you raised is the following: The witness has testified - and it's in his statement - that he sought to find out where the nine Serbs were, that he got the information that they could not be located. The witness now in many questions has said that he believed that a serious effort was made to locate them, and it seems that you want to put to the witness that this might not be actually what was done. But, of course, since it was not the witness who did it but since it was only the witness who received that answer, there are limits in putting to the witness that others had not done what the witness was told they had done. Would you please keep that in mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I believe that the witness did what he says he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Just one question in this respect: I was just trying to make a comparison. Had Mr. Izetbegovic been sitting at Pale, would he have known what the situation at Vogosca was? And that was my situation, and I believe that you are going to give me a true assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing we could ask the witness, Mr. Krajisnik, is the following: Whether the witness has any knowledge or any reason to know whether Mr. Izetbegovic, if he was in Pale, whether he would know what the situation in Vogosca was. It was -- it's, again, asking for a lot of speculation. You are not entitled to do that. Is it your view that Mr. Izetbegovic was in Pale, Mr. Krajisnik? If not, then it's a hypothetical question, which does not assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Momcilo Krajisnik was the one who was in Pale. And my question is, when I started talking about what happened in Sarajevo, I wanted the witness, since he is familiar with the situation, to say - because I believe that in spite of and above and beyond of the fact that he said that he would tell the truth, that he -- I wanted him to tell us what he thought I would know what was happening in Vogosca and other places. And I have one more question, because I don't want to waste the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Put that next question to the witness. Mr. Krajisnik, what you would have known or would not have known, the Chamber will determine that on the basis of the evidence, and it does not assist the Chamber to hear whether this witness thought it possible that someone at Pale would know something happening at either, 5, 10, 15, 50, or 100 kilometres away. That is established and determined on the basis of evidence, rather than on speculation by this witness. Please put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I do apologise. It's two questions, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that in these two books -- have you heard of it, I mean -- that they indicate that there were some proposals for exchanging Srebrenica and Vogosca and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I did hear rumours about it. I did not read it in these books, because I haven't read the books, but I did hear about such ideas or such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question: You mentioned that you heard that I was at Vogosca following an invitation from some people, and you saw other people visiting Vogosca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You were the president of the municipality. Have you ever invited me, as the president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to visit Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you whether you believe me or not, but I mean, those people who invited me were the ones who received my visits. Just one more question: Who did you exactly see at Vogosca? At what meeting? And in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from Mr. Ostojic, whom I saw in person - I don't know why he was there - I did not see any other people, such as Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic, and some others. I simply received that information according to which they occasionally visited Vogosca and were seen as guests in a restaurant between Vogosca and Hotonj in the direction of Sarajevo to the right. But I myself did not actually see them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Because I do actually have quite a few questions, but we don't have a lot of time, and I do thank the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Margetts, would you please keep in mind that we have a few questions, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. If I could present three documents to the witness and if those documents could be given exhibit numbers. The first document is a report for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document dated 06/03 1992 will be P744. The document dated 13/03 1992 will be Prosecution Exhibit P745. The third document, dated 12 November 1992, will be Prosecution Exhibit P746.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If Mr. Hasanovic could be shown the document P744.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: This is a report in relation to the security information in relation to events of the 1st of March, 2nd of March, 3rd, and 4th of March in Sarajevo, and it's compiled by the State Security Service of Sarajevo. Mr. Hasanovic, could you please refer to page 2 of the Bosnian document, and that's the last paragraph at page 2, which in the English is the first paragraph on page 3. This entry in this report reads as follows, Mr. Hasanovic. It says: "It was Serbs who first started setting up barricades, and the largest number of them were set up in a very short time; namely, from 2300 hours on 1st of March to 7.30 on 2nd of March. As a reaction and response to these barricades in the morning hours of the 2nd of March, Muslims also set up barricades." Is that consistent with your understanding of what occurred on the late evening of the 1st of March and the early hours of the 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, according to my information, it all tallies with what is in the document; that is to say, that it was the Serbs who set up the barricades first in reaction to the aforementioned referendum. And secondly, those barricades or checkpoints - and I do know that there were some barricades on the Muslim or Bosniak side, as well - were set up as a result of the barricades having been set up by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I explained to the Defence that the background information was, at that point, sufficiently dealt with. The witness has testified that there were, whether we call it barricades or checkpoints, on both sides of the city. There's really no need to go into the matter again because it's not essential for this case whether one party started at 12.00 at night and the other at 2.00 at night or it was just the other way around. That's not essential, I take it also, for your case. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that instance, it may be more appropriate, then, if these documents were introduced as contextual documents. Obviously if we could be given an opportunity to draw the Court's attention to those matters we consider relevant. But in light of Your Honour's comments, it may not be necessary for this witness to -- to respond to matters recorded in those documents and inform the Court whether they are consistent or not with his observations of -- of events that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, consistency, of course, with his testimony and with his statement, we can establish that ourselves. I mean, if a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness testifies that a car is red, and if a report says that it was a red car, then the consistency is really not something you would have to ask to the witness in order to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. I take it you have not seen these documents before?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, they were handed to me this morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But may I say we do not have any problem with the suggestion because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- we all know that this is just a device for putting in documents to ask the witness about consistency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And let's cut to the chase and get the documents put straight in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And I thank the Defence for that observation. And if we could proceed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So what we'll do is these documents are now tendered as contextual documents, and if there's any objection we'll hear after the Defence has had sufficient time to study them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have an objection at some point, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what's practical. I would have a few questions. Do you have any questions triggered by the -- well, the almost-non-questions, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. My observation doesn't -- it comes after the witness has gone. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you testified during these negotiations or during these talks you had on whether or not to split up Vogosca that you were trying to gain time, and you said it was mainly to find a safe place for, could I say, your people, and then were specifically asked also whether you needed time to arm the Muslims. You said yes, that was part of it as well. Could you tell us, if so, how the Muslims did arm themselves during this period.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that matter of arming the population is a very complex issue. All I can say for the time being is that that was done on the basis of purchases of a certain number of MTS, light armaments, light weapons, rifles, ammunition, and so on, and it was done for the most part through roundabout channels --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I --

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: And there were people somehow smuggling those weapons in, and the weapons were rather expensive. The prices were quite steep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Could you give us a rough estimate on how many rifles you obtained in this way to arm your local people.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an assessment because I wasn't involved in that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have an impression anyhow, even if you're not involved. I have impressions about a lot of things I'm not involved in.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I do have an estimate. In the area of Svrake and Semizovac, there were about 200 rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the heaviest kind of weaponry you managed to obtain?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Rifles. We only had rifles, and hand grenades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means no mortars?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: We did not have any initially, of course. And afterwards we could get some, and we managed to take some.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say "afterwards," what time frame are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Except -- I do apologise. When I say "later," what I mean is by the end of April. Some of that type of weaponry was sent to us from the nearby municipality of Visoko. So we had two mortars perhaps, and I don't know how many thousands of bullets, and that's all. And as far as the situation up until the 2nd of May was concerned, the municipality of Vogosca was still in some way not included in these combat or war activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No hand-held rockets?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that at all. That's a heavier type of weapon. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I've got one question to you: Did you ever learn anything about a relationship between Mr. Koprivica and the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Koprivica told me on several occasions and confirmed to me that he met quite often with SDS representatives. He also told me that he had quite a lot of contacts with Mr. Krajisnik. Krajisnik was a neighbour of ours who lived very close to Vogosca, a few kilometres from Vogosca actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And these contacts, did he further explain to you the kind of contacts, the content of it?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Koprivica tell you this when you met with him alone, or did he also say these kind of things in the presence of others?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he met with him alone or in the presence of others. I had quite regular contacts with Mr. Koprivica because our offices were adjacent and our contacts involved our business contacts, and in those contacts there were such conversations. Amongst other things, he told me what the shape of the future Yugoslavia would be, and he said, "The future shape of Yugoslavia would be determined by how far the Yugoslav People's Army reached." And I remember those words very well, and I quote him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is a rather general subject. You're just mentioning the future of Yugoslavia. You did not mention this in your earlier answers about relations with the leadership. May I take it that these conversations you had with Mr. Koprivica did not say anything about contacts with Mr. Krajisnik, in terms of contacts with SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I do not quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps my question was not quite clear. You told us that when the SDS party left the Municipal Assembly, that you were told that they were told by their leadership to do so. May I take it that in these conversations with Mr. Koprivica, not a similar relationship of someone when he talks about the future of Yugoslavia, talking in terms of what the leadership had in mind. Did he ever say anything about his thoughts in relation to what the SDS leadership took as their position?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From conversations between the two sides, if I may say so, one could conclude only that they had received instructions from their leadership, from the top; I've already mentioned that. I don't think that they would have done anything had they not received a request or an instruction to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say, "One could conclude only." On the basis of what would you conclude such a thing?

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of conversations of what they told us, their statements. When we asked them why they were withdrawing from the Assembly, what -- what the reason was, they could not give us any justifiable reason that would be applicable to Vogosca municipality and that would motivate them to walk out of the Assembly. And it is this fact that tells me that, in addition to their statements, they also had received instructions from their superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm now not talking any more about leaving the Assembly but more in general terms, conversations you had with Mr. Koprivica where he told you that he had a lot of contacts with Mr. Krajisnik. Did in these conversations ever -- was there ever discussed the specific, I would say, relation that you heard in the explanations that were given to you about leaving the Assembly? So apart from that, whether that ever in any other conversation with Mr. -- specifically with Mr. Koprivica and specifically in relation to Mr. Krajisnik, whether that ever came up.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we did not discuss anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BILAL HASANOVIC
utterances.text: -- of that sort. He did not provide me with any information as to what the topic of their conversation was. He only told me that they talked on a regular basis, but he never mentioned what was discussed, and I never insisted on him telling me what the topic of their discussion was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is there any very urgent matter at this moment? Because otherwise we'll adjourn. Another Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any very urgent matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honour. Your Honour had given us an instruction to distribute those dossiers by today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have those dossiers. We're prepared to distribute those, and we can ask Monday for exhibit numbers on that. We just want to inform the Court we're complying with a court order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Does any party insist on distributing them literally at this moment or that they'll be distributed through the building?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can live without them for several minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that has been settled. Any other very urgent matter, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn but not before having thanked the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, apologies, but the move for admission of exhibits for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we could do that on next Monday and not ask any further patience from the interpreters and the technicians. No, I thought you were about to join me in thanking the interpreters, Mr. Margetts, and that's certainly what was on your mind, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And I do join you in that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I know Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So do I, Your Honour. Your Honour, it's implicit. They know how much we appreciate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From time to time no doubt we should say it expressly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we also know that sometimes they have even more understanding on Fridays than on any other days. I see at least some smiles and some laughing. Thank you very much. We'll adjourn until next Monday, Madam Registrar, in the afternoon at quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 30th day of May, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
